title: Fraction Converter
context: Grade 5, the pages on converting between fractions and decimals. An adult sees a rule about counting zeros. What the pages are doing is linking tenths, hundredths and thousandths to the places after the point, so the denominator has to be 10, 100 or 1000 itself before the zeros are counted. Some fractions reach one of those by an equivalent fraction and some never do; one third never does.

writeup.why: Convert a fraction with a denominator of 10, 100 or 1000, or one that can be brought to it, into a decimal, and convert a decimal into a fraction in lowest terms.
writeup.look: A fraction card and a row of digit cards, a Zeros counter and a Count button under them, a Times both slider on the third phase and a Factors row on the last.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Fraction Converter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x sixty-four, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many digits have been counted from the right, one for each digit lit. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x sixty-four, y 202. The fraction card stands at x 110, y 240, 180 by 200, its numerator deep blue above the bar and its denominator in ink below. The digit cards run to its right from x 360 at y 280, each 80 across, one digit to a card, with room for grey zero cards to slide in at the front. The Zeros counter sits under the fraction card at y 470 and the Count button beside it at x 360. When the point drops it sits large and near-black between two cards, and the decimal is written green at y 400 under the row. The Times both slider runs along y 560 from x 110 to x 700, its handle showing the number both terms are multiplied by. On the last phase the Factors row runs along y 640, one chip for each common factor, the HCF lit amber. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across with a point key and a fraction bar key, for setting a fraction with a denominator up to 1000 or a decimal with up to three places, or for typing an answer into the slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. A decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it. The result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum, a difference or what is left, is green, with its shaded parts. Ten of one place traded for one of the next, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written after the point to line decimals up is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded part stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the decimal point is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label, Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left or Place holder, before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last fraction and its decimal side by side, the counted digits lit under the point.

phases.win: the point drops in front of the four, a grey 0 fills the ones place, and 0.43 is written in green

source_tool.description: A fraction card stands at the left of the working area, its numerator deep blue and its denominator in ink, and a row of digit cards to its right repeats the numerator one digit to a card. A Zeros counter under the card counts the zeros of the denominator one tap at a time. A Count button then sweeps that many digits from the right of the row, each lit amber as it is counted, and drops a large near-black point in front of them. When the numerator has fewer digits than the denominator has zeros, grey zero cards labelled Place holder slide in at the front of the row until the count is met, and a grey 0 drops into the ones place before the point. The decimal that results is written green under the row. The Count button is switched off for any denominator that is not 10, 100 or 1000 itself, and a Times both slider multiplies both terms by the same number, settling only when the denominator lands exactly on 10, 100 or 1000; for a denominator that never does, the slider runs to its end and the card says No such form. On the last phase a decimal on the digit cards goes back over 10, 100 or 1000, one zero for each digit after the point, and a Factors row lights the HCF of the two terms in amber to divide both by it. A number pad sets a fraction with a denominator up to 1000, or a decimal with up to three places. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many digits have been counted.
source_tool.art_direction: Number cards and a dot card / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: strips cut into ten equal parts, hundred grids of ten rows and ten columns, place value charts with a column for each place, column sums with their points in one line, and measuring jugs, ropes and scales marked in tenths.

Every whole is drawn the same size as every other whole it is compared or combined with, and its parts are exactly equal: a strip in tenths has ten parts of one width, and a hundred grid is always a full ten by ten.
The decimal point is drawn large and always sits between the ones and the tenths. In a column, every point lies on one vertical line.
A place value chart names every column above its digit: Hundreds, Tens, Ones, the point, Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths.
Where shaded cells are counted, exactly the stated number is shaded, and they stay countable at a glance.

Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a strip cutting into tenths, ten tenths sliding together into one whole, a zero appearing after the point, or a carry moving to the next place.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit or a part the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a decimal plays in a piece of working: every decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it, and every result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum or a difference, is green, with its shaded parts; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Ten of one place traded for one of the next place, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written at the end, after the point, to make like decimals is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey. An unshaded part of a whole stays warm white inside its outline, and the decimal point itself is near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count the zeros at the bottom again, then count that many digits.
voice.onNext: A new fraction. Look at the bottom number first.
voice.opening: A fraction, and a row of digit cards waiting for a point.
voice.onFinish: The zeros told you where the point goes, every time.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Pick your own fraction or decimal, and turn it either way.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has laid number cards over 10, 100 or 1000 and placed a dot card by hand. The tool is what counts the places one card at a time and slides zero cards in front of a short numerator, and what refuses to count a denominator that is not 10, 100 or 1000.

answer_key.rule: A fraction whose denominator is 10, 100 or 1000 itself becomes a decimal by counting: the number of zeros in the denominator is the number of digits after the point. Count that many digits from the right of the numerator and put the point before them. If the numerator is too short, write zeros in front of it, and write 0 in the ones place if nothing is left before the point. Any other denominator is first changed by an equivalent fraction, multiplying both terms by the same number, and that works only when the denominator goes exactly into 10, 100 or 1000. Not every fraction can be written this way: 1/3 has no such form. To go back, write the digits without the point over 1 followed by as many zeros as there are digits after the point, then divide both terms by their HCF.
answer_key.wrong: The digit cards are counted again from the right, one at a time, with the child's decimal built beside them as a second row, so the child sees where its point sits against the counted one. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The denominator 100 has two zeros, so two digits come after the point.
Count two digits from the right of 67 and put the point before them.
Nothing is left before the point, so write 0 in the ones place.
items.question: Write 67/100 as a decimal.
items.checkpoint: The number of zeros in the denominator is the number of digits after the point.
items.misconception: Writing 6.7, which puts only one digit after the point though 100 has two zeros.

steps: The whole number 9 stays before the point.
1000 has three zeros, so three digits come after the point.
7 has only one digit, so write two zeros in front of it: 007.
items.question: Write 9 7/1000 as a decimal.
items.checkpoint: When the numerator is too short, write zeros in front of it.
items.misconception: Writing 9.7, which leaves out the two zeros in front and turns seven thousandths into seven tenths.

steps: 20 is not 10, 100 or 1000, so the zeros cannot be counted yet.
items.question: Write 7/20 as a decimal.
items.checkpoint: Make the denominator 10, 100 or 1000 itself before counting zeros.
items.misconception: Counting the one zero of 20 and writing 0.7, which is seven tenths and twice as much as 7/20.

steps: Write the digits without the point: 435.
There are two digits after the point, so the denominator is 100: 4.35 = 435/100.
435 divided by 5 is 87, and 100 divided by 5 is 20, so 4.35 = 87/20.
items.question: Write 4.35 as a fraction in lowest terms.
items.checkpoint: A decimal goes over 1 with one zero for each digit after the point, then is divided by the HCF.
items.misconception: Stopping at 435/100, which is equal but not in lowest terms, since 435 and 100 still share the factor 5.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Write 6/100 as a decimal.
items.final_answer: 0.06. 100 has two zeros, so a zero goes in front of the 6

items.question: Write 3 41/1000 as a decimal.
items.final_answer: 3.041. 1000 has three zeros, so a zero goes in front of 41

items.question: Write 0.8 as a fraction in lowest terms.
items.final_answer: 4/5. 0.8 = 8/10, and dividing both terms by their HCF, 2, gives 4/5

items.question: Can 1/6 be written with a denominator of 10, 100 or 1000? Explain.
items.final_answer: No. 6 does not go exactly into 10, 100 or 1000, so 1/6 has no such form

items.question: Write 12.05 as a fraction in lowest terms.
items.final_answer: 241/20. 12.05 = 1205/100, and dividing both terms by their HCF, 5, gives 241/20

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

teaching_notes: Count the zeros of the denominator aloud before any digit is moved. Only 10, 100 or 1000 itself will do: a denominator that merely ends in a zero, such as 20, is first changed by an equivalent fraction. When the numerator is too short, write zeros in front of it, and a 0 in the ones place if nothing is left. Some fractions, such as one third, never reach 10, 100 or 1000; say so and leave them there. Going back, the number of digits after the point gives the number of zeros in the denominator, and the HCF gives lowest terms.
generation_prompt: Build a fraction to decimal tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A fraction card stands at the left of the working area, its numerator deep blue, with a row of digit cards to its right, one digit to a card. A Zeros counter counts the zeros of the denominator. A Count button sweeps that many digits from the right, each lit amber, and drops a large near-black point in front of them; when the numerator is too short, grey zero cards labelled Place holder slide in at the front and a grey 0 fills the ones place. The result is written green. The Count button is off unless the denominator is 10, 100 or 1000 itself; a Times both slider multiplies both terms and settles only on 10, 100 or 1000, and for a denominator that never does the card says No such form. On the last phase a Back button writes a decimal over 10, 100 or 1000 and a Factors row lights the HCF in amber. A number pad. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of digits counted. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Count the zeros at the bottom. That many digits go after the point. Fill any gap with zeros in front.
